q: What does a load balancer do vs an API gateway?
a: A load balancer spreads traffic across identical instances and skips unhealthy ones. An API gateway is the front door: authentication, rate limiting, routing to different services, logging. Often both are used.
So any instance can serve any request: you can add instances to scale, and a crash loses nothing. Sessions, history and agent state live in Redis or a database.

Start with a modular monolith for speed and simplicity; split out components with different scaling or hardware needs (GPU model serving, ingestion workers) or separate team ownership. Microservices add network latency and operational complexity.

q: When would you use a queue?
a: For slow, bursty or non-urgent work the user shouldn't wait for: document ingestion, batch scoring, long agent runs, notifications. Queues absorb spikes and decouple producers from workers.

After repeated failures from a dependency, stop calling it for a while and use a fallback (cache, simpler model, friendly error), then test it again. Prevents cascading failures and wasted time on timeouts.

q: What does idempotent mean and why does it matter?
a: Doing an operation twice has the same effect as once. Retries are only safe for idempotent operations; for side effects (payments, emails) use idempotency keys.
